av_event.what: Before answering, Kirsty looks down and away from the screen to her left for about four seconds with her lips pressed together, then looks back at the camera and starts speaking.

text:
B: Hello? Hi, can you hear me okay?
A: Yeah. Hi. Sorry, it took a second to come on.
B: That's okay. I'm Kasia. It says Katarzyna on there, but nobody calls me that except my mum when I'm in trouble.
A: Oh. I'm Kirsty. Erm, nice to meet you.
B: You too. Where are you?
A: Burnley. What about you?
B: Warrington. Originally Poland, but I've been in Warrington years now.
A: Oh, right. Is it nice, Warrington?
B: It's... fine. My husband grew up there, so I have to say yes. The M62 is not nice.
A: No. Our kid drives it sometimes, from Blackburn. He's always moaning about it.
B: Everyone moans about it. Erm, so what do you do, Kirsty?
A: Erm. I'm not working at the minute. I was at a food factory, on the line, packing, for nine years, and they cut a shift last year, so. I'm applying for things. Warehouse, mainly.
B: Nine years is a long time. It's hard when it ends like that, not because of you.
A: Yeah. It's alright. What about you?
B: I work in a hospital lab, haematology. Blood, basically. I look at blood films under the microscope, check the analysers, sign off results. And I train the new ones, which I like most, actually.
A: I used to train new starters. One at a time. I was terrified every time, but they all stayed, so.
B: That's the best proof, isn't it? If they stay. People think training is talking a lot, but mostly it's being patient and letting them make the small mistake so they don't make the big one. Sorry, what I mean is, you watch, you don't take over.
A: Yeah. That's what I did. I'd just stand next to them and not say owt unless they were about to put the wrong label on.
B: Exactly that. Erm, I saw a cat in your picture?
A: Yeah, Moss. She's ancient. She knocks things off the windowsill every morning. I think she thinks it's her job.
B: No! Mine does exactly the same. Bodzio. He's a rescue and a bit fat, and he looks at you while he pushes it. Last week it was a little pot of basil, soil everywhere.
A: They do look at you, don't they? Moss did a jar of pencils this morning. Is that Polish, Bodzio?
B: Yes, it's sort of short for Bogdan. It's a very old-man name. My husband wanted Kevin.
A: Kevin's quite good for a cat, to be fair.
B: Ha. Don't tell him that. So you draw? The pencils, and there was a picture on the wall.
A: Yeah, a bit. That one's the canal lock near me. I do the mills and the chimneys mostly. There's one at the end of my road, it's the only one left of about six that used to be round there. And sometimes I go up by Pendle Hill and do the farms and the walls. I don't know, it's something to do with my hands. It stops me thinking too much.
B: That's a nice reason. I do word puzzles on my phone for the same thing, but it's less beautiful.
A: Erm, can I ask, sorry, I noticed your cross. Do you go to church?
B: Not every week. I'm Catholic. I go to the Polish Mass at Christmas and Easter, and an English one otherwise. You?
A: Most Sundays. The early one. I sit at the back.
B: The back is the best place. Nobody asks you to help with the coffee.
A: That's exactly why, yeah.
B: Oh, is that the timer already?
